supplement.where: Appendices A to G follow the main text in this PDF (PDF pp. 44-117, printed appendix pp. 1-74). Survey flows for the control and partial-treatment conditions are 'available upon request' (PDF p. 44).
supplement.holds: Arm-level pairwise differences with SEs (Table A.3), robustness tables (A.4, A.5, F.2-F.4), continue-option outcomes (D.1, D.2), broad-option outcome (D.5), problem-statement similarity (Figure E.1), category counts (E.5-E.8), preregistered outcomes (F.5), attrition (F.1), follow-up team study (Appendix G, Table G.2). Nothing needed for extraction is outside this PDF.

paper_design_summary: In a classroom exercise in a core MBA strategy course, 305 MBA students analyzed a pre-distributed business case (Rated) and wrote a problem formulation, then generated strategic options, then picked the best option. Students were randomized (stratified by section, gender, and consulting background) to no LLM (control), a GPT-4-based LLM from the ideation stage onward (partial treatment), or a GPT-4-based LLM from the problem-formulation stage onward (full treatment). Outcomes are computed on each student's submitted options: number of options, number and share of options a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 classifier codes as strategic versus operational, and whether the chosen option is strategic. A follow-up study randomized 24 teams of executives (96 people) to full versus partial LLM timing and is used mainly for qualitative evidence.

participants.exclusions: Appendix F: the assigned sample was 338 (336 preregistered plus two students initially categorized as 'partners'); 305 participated and 33 were absent. eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned individual MBA students (stratified) to no LLM, GPT-4 from ideation onward, or GPT-4 from problem formulation onward (PDF p. 13); 305 people analyzed of 338 assigned (PDF p. 105). Outcomes are computed on submitted options: number of options (fluency), categories covered (flexibility), and LLM-classified strategic share. The creativity constructs are fluency and flexibility only; no novelty or creativity rating, and the paper's main construct (strategic focus) is 'other'. Strategic-option generation for a business case is treated here as idea generation. S2 (96 executives, 24 teams, full vs partial AI timing) also randomizes AI configuration but is presented as qualitative.

one_line_finding: Relative to no AI, GPT-4 access from problem formulation onward raised the number of options by 1.55 (SE 0.43; control mean 5.68) but lowered the strategic share by 0.07 (SE 0.03) and the chance of choosing a strategic option by 0.15 (SE 0.07); access from ideation onward raised options by 2.68 (SE 0.55) with no change in strategic share (PDF p. 38, Table 2).
open_questions: Design class: the main experiment is an in-class exercise in a core MBA strategy course (case discussed in class); coded field_rct under the codebook's 'coursework' definition, but the paper calls it 'classroom-based' and 'laboratory-style', so lab_rct is defensible. Same question for the executive-education follow-up (S2).

Is strategic-option generation for a business case a creative/ideation task in scope? The paper contrasts its strategy outcomes with 'creativity-based metrics such as novelty, quantity, and diversity' (PDF p. 5, Section 1; also PDF p. 28) but does report quantity (fluency).

Primary record for with_ai: the only creativity construct with participant-level SEs is number of options (fluency); rule 3 would pick the full-treatment arm (AI throughout) as closest to free chatbot use.
S2 measure codes for strategic and continue options are not stated in Appendix G; measure code 'automated_score' there is a placeholder.
Randomized counts by arm for the 338 assigned students are not printed; only the 305 participants by arm (103/102/100).
notes: Discrepancies in the document: (1) the interaction-log subsample is 47 full / 41 partial in the text (PDF p. 14, p. 80) and Table A.6, but Table A.1 Panel (b) prints Partial 47 / Full 41 (PDF p. 55). (2) Table G.2 labels the difference column '(3)-(2)' (Partial minus Full) but the printed b values equal Full minus Partial. (3) Main text says option coding details are in 'Appendix A' (PDF p. 15) but they are in Appendix C. (4) Text p-values for treatment vs control (e.g. 0.042 for strategic share) come from the stratified regressions; Table A.3 raw differences give different p-values (0.060). Outcomes left out of the list: semantic similarity of problem statements to the participant's own LLM interactions (Table E.9, beta 0.064 (0.016), N = 88, full vs partial) and 15-gram reliance on LLM text (32.7% vs 55.6%, p = 0.0176), which measure AI reliance rather than creativity; time measures (Tables 4, 6); math-question accuracy; first-vs-last option strategic change and option-level multilevel logit (Table 6 cols 6-7, 1,591 options); individual category binaries (Tables E.5, E.6 cols 2-11); overlap measures other than option-only categories (Tables E.7, E.8); heterogeneity tables E.10-E.14 and Table E.3.
